title: The Library Cart Parade
premise: Mayor Mallow boasts that the library parade will be the biggest ever. Juniper, a child librarian, wants every small reader to find a book; Bram, a cheerful cart builder, wants his new rolling cart admired. One shared cart, a town square, and three changing starting conditions turn the mayor’s boast into very different parades.
cast_and_props: Characters: Mayor Mallow (wants applause and a huge crowd), Juniper (wants books to reach overlooked readers), Bram (wants his cart to earn a ridiculous prize), and Pip the library cart (prop, with shelves, owner, location, decoration, and cargo slots). Setting: the library, its front square, and the lane beside it. Props: the shared cart, a bell, a banner, and book bundles. Keep all state scalar; every key begins with an entity ID.
kernels_and_interactions: Use 4 kernel families: movement/location, ownership and loading, knowledge through observe/tell, and performance/audience response. Juniper can observe the cart’s cargo or a lane sign, then tell Mayor or Bram; this knowledge must enable the correct loading or route choice. Transfer handles book bundles or the banner. A parade scene changes cart.location and audience response only after the cart is actually decorated and loaded. A pivotal scene changes Mayor’s belief or Juniper’s confidence, and that turn must affect which completion is reachable. No abstract score counters.
seed_parameters: Declare initial premise keys such as cart.cargo, cart.owner, cart.location, mayor.knows.lane, and juniper.motive. Seed 1: the cart is empty, the mayor insists on a grand lap, and Juniper has noticed the lane beside the library. Seed 2: the cart is already loaded with picture books, but Mayor believes the bundles are party decorations and demands they be hidden. Seed 3: Bram has promised the cart’s bell to a distant guest, while Juniper has invited quiet readers to the square; the conflicting promises must be discovered through observation or telling. Use rng only for harmless prose variation and candidate weights, not route selection.
candidate_scenes: Create 16–19 candidates, with 5–10 selected. Shared scenes: Juniper inspects the cart; Juniper tells Mayor or Bram what she learned; Bram decorates the cart; the cart rolls into the square; the audience responds. Problem-specific scenes: (1) Juniper observes that the narrow lane leads to readers who cannot reach the square, then persuades Mayor to make a small, useful book parade there; completion is cart.cargo == books, cart.location == lane, audience.response == delighted. (2) Mayor orders the loaded picture books covered as parade junk; Juniper opens a bundle, reveals the books, and Mayor must choose a “book rain” distribution; completion is books distributed and children reading in the square. (3) Bram learns his bell promise conflicts with Juniper’s quiet-reader invitation; he trades the bell for a banner or performs a silent ribbon parade; completion is cart.decorated == banner, audience.response == welcoming, and quiet_guest == included. Reuse preparation, reveal, decorating, rolling, and audience scenes across paths. The inciting action must be an observed lane, an explicit mayoral order, or Bram’s bell promise before any response.
constraints: Goal must require a completed parade and audience response, not a selected style or plan. Track concrete location, cargo, ownership, decoration, invitation, belief, and response. Supply every candidate with catalog prose, including preview-only cards. Openings must be guarded by the actual seed conditions and name the specific desire/problem. Use bridge cards for routine loading, walking, and banner tying; use beat cards for discovery, disagreement, choice, and audience reaction. Never let a character speak a fact before learning it. Use 1–2 pivotal actions only. premise_keys: cart.cargo, cart.location, mayor.knows.lane, bram.promise. outcome_keys: cart.location, cart.cargo, audience.response.
different_endings: Ending A: the cart appears in the narrow lane, books rise from its shelves, and readers who missed the grand square parade wave from doorways. Ending B: Mayor’s enormous banner droops while children sit on the square stones reading picture books; the boast has become a book-sharing parade. Ending C: the cart rolls silently beneath ribbons, and the once-worried quiet guests begin a tiny walking library, bell-free but full of smiles. Give each ending at least two guarded variants, with the final image carrying the meaning rather than an explanation.
